passages.text: And when I, Clement, heard this, I said, “Truly I rejoice and acknowledge my gratitude to God, the benefactor in every respect. Yet he himself knows that I shall not be able to think anything except to think about everything in God’s favor. Therefore, do not suppose that I am asking because I doubt what has been said by God or even what will yet be said, but so that, once I too have learned, I may be able to teach another who wishes to learn in a fair-minded way. So tell me what false things have been added to the Scriptures and how they prove to be actually false.” And Peter answered, “Even if you had not asked me, as I proceeded through the arguments in their proper order, I would have supplied the demonstration I promised. Nevertheless, hear how the Scriptures tell many falsehoods about him, as you will discover when you read them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: God, the benefactor in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ πάντα presents God as beneficent in every respect, rather than merely identifying him as the benefactor of all things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to think about everything in God’s favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπὲρ θεοῦ indicates thought favorable to or in defense of God; an alternative is “to hold every opinion in defense of God.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who wishes to learn in a fair-minded way
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐγνωμόνως can describe a reasonable, well-disposed, or appreciative manner; “fair-minded” suits the prospective learner’s disposition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what false things have been added to the Scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσκείμενα describes material placed alongside or added to the writings; the context treats γραφαί as authoritative Scriptures.

lexical_decisions.chosen: how they prove to be actually false
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual combination πῶς ὅτι is understood as asking how the alleged additions turn out in fact to be false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Scriptures tell many falsehoods about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταψεύδομαι with the genitive means to speak falsely about or against someone; “him” refers contextually to God.
ἐντυγχάνω with writings commonly means to encounter them by reading; a more literal alternative is “when you engage with them.”

passages.text: The things about to be said will suffice by way of example. I do not think, my friend Clement, that anyone who retains even a little affection and gratitude toward God will be able to accept, or so much as hear, the things said against him. But how is it possible for anyone to have a soul devoted to one sovereign and to become devout after having assumed beforehand that there are many gods and not one? And even if there is one, who, finding him amid many absurdities, will strive to become devout, in the hope that the origin of all things, because of the absurdities inherent in his own nature, will not pursue the wrongdoings of others?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ οἶμαι δέ, ὦ φίλε Κλήμης, εἰ δυνήσεταί τις
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not think, my friend Clement, that anyone ... will be able
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although εἰ can formally introduce “whether,” after negative οἶμαι the contextual force is an emphatic doubt that anyone could do so.
στοργή denotes affectionate attachment, while εὐγνωμοσύνη here naturally denotes grateful appreciation toward God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a soul devoted to one sovereign
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “a monarchic soul,” the phrase describes a disposition affirming sole divine sovereignty; “monotheistic soul” is possible but would replace the author’s monarchy imagery.
The participle denotes adopting a prior conception or assumption.
“God” is elliptically understood from the preceding contrast between many gods and one.
The phrase portrays God as being found in or associated with numerous incongruities; “finding him implicated in many absurdities” is another possible rendering.
ἀρχή may mean origin, first principle, or ruler; “origin” fits God as the source of everything, while “ruler of all” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will not pursue the wrongdoings of others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπέρχομαι can mean to come against, visit, or pursue; the context may specifically imply calling others to account or punishing their wrongdoings.

passages.text: Therefore, far be it from us to believe either that the Master of all, “who created heaven and earth” and everything in them, shares sovereignty with others, or that he lies—for if he lies, who then tells the truth?—or that he “tests” as though ignorant—and who then has foreknowledge? If he “deliberates” and “changes his mind,” who then is perfect in understanding and steadfast in purpose? If he “is jealous,” who then is beyond comparison? If he “hardens hearts,” who then makes wise? If there are blind and deaf people, who then has granted sight and hearing? If he advises defrauding, who then practices justice? If he “mocks,” who then is sincere? If he is unable, who then can do all things? If he acts unjustly, who then is just? If he “creates evils,” who then will do good things? If he does evil things, who then does good things?

lexical_decisions.chosen: far be it from us to believe
lexical_decisions.rationale: The impersonal optative expresses emphatic rejection; “from us” is supplied by the conventional English construction without identifying a narrower subject.
συνάρχω means to rule jointly with others, not merely to coexist with them.
πειράζω may mean test or tempt; the accompanying comparison with ignorance makes testing to discover unknown information the relevant idea.
The verb can mean considers, reflects, or deliberates; “deliberates” highlights the alleged lack of already perfected understanding.
The verb may mean regrets or changes one’s mind; the contrast with being steadfast in purpose favors the latter here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If there are blind and deaf people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek contains plural adjectives without an expressed noun or verb. This rendering treats them substantivally and supplies only the English existential construction; context may instead imply “if [he makes people] blind and deaf.”
νομιτεύω can mean to observe something as customary or lawful; “regards justice as law” is also possible.
The verb denotes mocking or making sport of someone; “deceives” is possible in some contexts but is not required here.
The verb denotes inability; the following contrast is with the one who can do all things.
The rendering preserves both the creation verb and the plural substantive κακά rather than generalizing the claim as merely “causes evil.”

source_issues.issue: The clause has plural predicate adjectives but no expressed subject or finite verb. It is defensibly read as an elliptical nominal clause, though the context may imply an omitted action such as making people blind and deaf. No restoration is inserted into the translation.
The supplied print uses the unassimilated spelling ἐνπαίζει where the normalized spelling is commonly ἐμπαίζει. The printed form remains intelligible and is not altered.
An isolated high mark appears between καὶ and τίς. It has no evident syntactic function and is most plausibly editorial or typographical punctuation.

passages.text: If he desires “the fat mountain,” to whom do all things belong? If he lies, who then tells the truth? If he dwells in a tent, who then is uncontainable? If he longs for fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations, who then needs nothing, and who is holy, and who is pure, and who is perfect? If he delights in lamps and lampstands, who then set the luminaries in heaven? If he dwells with thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke, who then, being light, illuminates the greatest age? If he approaches with trumpets and loud cries and missiles and arrows, who then is the calm awaited by all? If he himself loves wars, who then desires peace? If he himself creates “the evils,” who then fashions good things? If he himself is without affection, who then loves humanity? If he himself is not faithful concerning what he promises, who then will be trusted? If he himself loves wicked people and adulterers and murderers, who then will be a just judge? If he himself changes his mind, who then is steadfast? If he himself chooses evil people, who then welcomes good people?

lexical_decisions.rationale: πῖον literally describes something fat or rich and may imply a fertile or luxuriant mountain; the concrete “fat” image is retained because the phrase is quoted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom do all things belong
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “and whose are all things?” the question challenges the attribution of desire to the one who owns everything.
The adjective denotes one who cannot be contained, confined, or accommodated within a place.
κνίση denotes the greasy smoke or savor rising from burning fat; the compact rendering preserves both the material and sacrificial imagery.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κνίσης καὶ θυσιῶν καὶ θυμάτων καὶ προσχύσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: fat-smoke and sacrifices and sacrificial victims and libations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated conjunctions and the distinction between sacrifices, victims, and poured offerings are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν γνόφῳ καὶ σκότῳ καὶ θυέλλῃ καὶ καπνῷ σύνεστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: dwells with thick gloom and darkness and tempest and smoke
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύνεστιν literally means “is together with”; “dwells with” conveys association while preserving all four atmospheric images.
αἰών may denote an age, eternity, or a world-order. “Age” is the most direct rendering, while “the greatest world” remains a possible contextual interpretation.
βολίδες are thrown projectiles or bolts, while τοξεύματα are things shot from a bow; the two images are kept distinct.
προσδόκιμος means expected or awaited, and τῶν ὅλων can refer either to everyone or collectively to all things.
The adjective denotes absence of natural or familial affection; “unloving” is a broader alternative.
Here the verb is contrasted with βέβαιος, one who is stable or steadfast; “regrets” is also lexically possible.
The verb can mean admits, receives, or accepts; “welcomes” provides a natural contrast with choosing evil people.
